title: Microscopic Evidence for Early Cancer Treatment
content: Examination of ancient bones has established that cancer has existed in humans for centuries. However, a recent study by Tatiana Tondini, Albert Isidro, and Edgard Camarós provided what appears to be the earliest evidence for surgery on a bone cancer, and possibly exploration of a tumor soon after death [1]. They examined two skulls from ancient Egypt. One was from a female over 50 years of age from the Late Period (664–343 BCE), and the other was from a male 30–35 years of age from the Old Kingdom (2,687–2,345 BCE). There was also a mandible from this male. Lesions were characterized and diagnoses were made based on micro-CT scanning (μCT) and light microscopy surface analysis. Importantly, Tondini et al. showed how a methodological implementation of only non-destructive techniques can lead to significant discoveries.
